The question of whether fish oil improves brain function is contested, with research outcomes pointing in different directions. Some sources support a benefit, while credible sources find no improvement from supplementation specifically.

On the supportive side, a PubMed-indexed study states that DHA "is also required for maintenance of normal brain function in adults" and that "the inclusion of plentiful DHA in the diet improves learning ability," with deficiencies linked to cognitive decline and Alzheimer's disease [d5]. A 2015 review of 28 studies cited by Healthline found that adults with mild memory loss who took DHA and EPA supplements "experienced improved episodic memory" [d2], and other sources suggest fish oil can boost BDNF, a protein that triggers new brain cell production and may improve cognitive function [d3].

On the other hand, Harvard Health (a high-credibility source) concludes that "omega-3 supplements haven't shown the same effect" as eating fish, stating that "any benefit seems to come from a greater intake of fish and not from taking fish oil supplements" [d4]. WebMD similarly states that "taking fish oil supplements by mouth does not improve most memory or thinking skills in older people, young adults, or children" [d7]. Additionally, d3 notes that the omega-6 to omega-3 imbalance in western diets means "most people do not receive many benefits from fish oil supplements" [d3].

In summary, while DHA as a nutrient appears important for brain health [d5], the evidence from randomized clinical trials and systematic reviews does not consistently support that fish oil supplements improve brain function, with high-credibility sources [d4][d7] finding no clear cognitive benefit from supplementation alone.
